summary: This informational memo advises TCP implementers on sharing connection state, such as what is kept in a TCP Control Block, among similar concurrent or consecutive connections. The goal is to help new connections reach steady-state operation faster without breaking interoperability. It updates and replaces RFC 2140's description of this sharing.

plainLanguage.summary: When you start a new connection, the first few packets are sent slowly because the two ends have to learn how fast the network is. This memo describes how a computer can remember what it learned on an earlier or parallel connection to the same place, and start the new connection at that speed instead.

questions: what is a tcp control block
what is temporal sharing in tcp
what is ensemble sharing in tcp
subtitle: How TCP connections to the same host can reuse what earlier or parallel connections learned.

tldr.problem: Each TCP connection normally learns about its network path from scratch, which slows down the many short-lived connections used by the Web.
tldr.mechanism: Implementations can keep a cache of TCP Control Block values per host pair and use it to initialize new connections, either from past ones (temporal sharing) or from concurrent ones (ensemble sharing).
tldr.outcome: Sharing affects only how a connection starts, so it does not change TCP's long-term behavior or interoperability. This memo replaces RFC 2140.

facts.label: Shareable congestion window
facts.value: Not shared in the surveyed implementations

today: RFC 9040 is an Informational memo that obsoletes RFC 2140, and no later RFC is recorded as replacing it. It updates the earlier description of TCP state sharing, adds sections on compatibility and implementation observations, and discusses adapting the initial window automatically.

sections.title: Introduction: Why Share TCP State
sections.content:
TCP is a connection-oriented reliable transport protocol layered over IP. Each TCP connection maintains state, usually in a data structure called the TCP Control Block, which contains information about the connection state, its associated local process, and feedback parameters about the connection's transmission properties. As originally specified and usually implemented, most of this information is maintained on a per-connection basis. Some implementations share certain information across connections to the same host, which is intended to lead to better overall transient performance, especially for the numerous short-lived and simultaneous connections used by the World Wide Web. The point of sharing is to help connections converge to long-term steady-state behaviour more quickly without affecting interoperability.

This document updates and replaces RFC 2140's discussion of state sharing. Because sharing affects only the initialization of a connection, it has no effect on the long-term behaviour of TCP once a connection is established, and none on interoperability. Sharing path information across SYN destination ports assumes that TCP segments between the same host pair experience the same path properties, that is, that traffic is not routed differently based on port numbers or other connection parameters.

The document notes that the observations about sharing apply similarly to any protocol with congestion state, including SCTP and DCCP, and to the individual subflows of Multipath TCP. Its core describes behaviour that is already permitted by the TCP standards, so the document gives informative guidance and uses normative language only in Appendix C, as examples of requirements for future consideration.
sections.plainLanguage: Every new TCP connection starts by feeling its way: it sends a little, measures, and speeds up. If the computer already knows how the path to that place behaved last time, the new connection can skip the slow part. That is all this memo is about.

sections.title: The TCP Control Block and What May Be Shared
sections.content:
A TCP Control Block describes the data associated with each connection, that is, with each association of a pair of applications across the network. It contains at least the local process state, meaning pointers to the send and receive buffers, to the retransmission queue and current segment, and to the IP protocol control block, together with per-connection shared state. That per-connection state is shown as split into macro-state and micro-state. Macro-state describes the protocol for establishing the initial shared state about the connection, and includes the endpoint numbers and the components, such as timers and flags, required upon commencement. Micro-state describes the protocol after a connection has been established, maintaining the reliability and congestion control of the data transferred.

Two other classes of shared micro-state are associated more with host pairs than with application pairs. One class is clearly host-pair dependent, such as sendMSS, MMS_R, MMS_S and PMTU, because these are defined by the endpoint or endpoint pair or are already cached on that basis. The other is host-pair dependent in its aggregate, such as congestion window information and current window sizes, because they depend on the total capacity between the two endpoints.

Not all of the state is necessarily shareable. Some TCP options are negotiated only on request by the application layer, so their use may not be correlated across connections, and other options negotiate connection-specific parameters, which are similarly not shareable. The receive window is excluded from further discussion because its value should depend on the send window size, so it is already addressed by send window sharing.
sections.plainLanguage: The per-connection record holds two sorts of things. Some describe the application on this end, and cannot be shared. Others describe the path to the other end, and can be, because the path is the same however the connection is used.

sections.title: Temporal Sharing and Ensemble Sharing
sections.content:
There are two cases of interdependence. Temporal sharing occurs when the TCB of an earlier, now closed, connection to a host is used to initialize some parameters of a new connection to that same host, that is, in sequence. Ensemble sharing occurs when a currently active connection to a host is used to initialize another, concurrent, connection to that host. The cache is read to initialize new TCBs and written when more current per-host state is available.

For temporal sharing, a new connection can be initialized with the cached maximum message sizes, the cached sendMSS, PMTU, RTT and its variation, the cached slow-start threshold and the cached send-side congestion window, while option-specific information such as the TCP Fast Open cookie and a record of a failed Fast Open attempt is copied as well. The cache is updated mostly when a connection closes: the round-trip time and its variation, the slow-start threshold and the congestion window are merged with the cached values, where the merge function may be a windowed average or an exponential decay of the form new equals (1 minus alpha) times old plus alpha times new. The maximum message sizes are reported by the local IP stack, so caching them is of little value; the PMTU is cached at the IP layer and updated after path MTU discovery; and sendMSS is updated when the MSS option is received in a SYN.

Ensemble sharing needs more care, because some shared state acts in aggregate. MSS and RTT values can be copied, but it is not appropriate to copy the congestion window or the slow-start threshold; instead, the new values are a function of the cumulative values and the number of connections. The cache should be updated as early as possible, sometimes before a connection is closed, otherwise opening several concurrent connections may produce no sharing at all. The document notes that current TCP implementations initialize the congestion window to 4 segments as standard and 10 segments experimentally, that an algorithm exists that adjusts the initial window depending on the window values of ongoing connections, and that sharing mechanisms over long timescales can adapt the initial window automatically.
sections.plainLanguage: There are two ways to share. You can use what an earlier connection learned, or what a connection running right now has learned. With several connections at once, the numbers that describe the shared capacity have to be divided between them rather than copied.

sections.title: Problems with Sharing
sections.content:
For the congestion and current window information, the initial values computed by sharing may not be consistent with the long-term aggregate behaviour of a set of concurrent connections between the same endpoints. If the congestion window of a single existing connection has converged to 40 segments, two newly joining connections will assume initial windows of 10 segments and the existing connection's window will not decrease to accommodate the additional load, so the three connections can mutually interfere. One example is seen on low-bandwidth, high-delay links, where concurrent connections supporting Web traffic can collide because their initial windows were too large, even when set at one segment. Some studies suggest that sharing the slow-start threshold between short flows can deteriorate the performance of individual connections, although this may benefit aggregate network performance.

TCP is sometimes used where packets of the same host pair do not always take the same path, for instance when connection-specific parameters are used for routing, or where multipath routing examines transport headers. Traversing the same path is not important for host-specific information or for information already cached per host, such as the path MTU. Where information is shared across different SYN destination ports, path-related information can be incorrect, but the impact may be small because sharing affects only the transient event of a connection start. In the case of temporal sharing, cached information can also become invalid over time, so the mechanisms that address idle TCP connections could also be applied to cache management.

It can be wrong to share information between connections on the same host as identified by IP address if an address is assigned to a new host, as with address spinning used by providers to inhibit running servers, or if NAT, NAPT or any other address-sharing mechanism is used, although such mechanisms are less likely with IPv6. Some of the information is about dominant path properties rather than the specific host, so addresses may differ while the relevant part of the path is the same.
sections.plainLanguage: Sharing is only safe when the two connections really do travel the same way. If a network sends different traffic over different paths, or if an address is handed to a different machine, the remembered numbers can be wrong.

sections.title: What Implementations Do Today
sections.content:
The observation that some TCB state is host-pair specific rather than application-pair dependent is not new, and is a common engineering decision in layered protocol implementations. Although now deprecated, T/TCP was the first to propose using caches in order to maintain TCB states, and at least one T/TCP implementation saved the MSS and aggregated the RTT parameters across multiple connections while omitting the congestion window information. Temporal sharing of cached TCB data was originally implemented in the Sun OS 4.1.3 T/TCP extensions and the FreeBSD port of the same.

The document's table describes the implementation status for temporal sharing in Windows as of December 2020, the Apple variants as of January 2021, Linux kernel version 5.10.3 and FreeBSD 12, and states that ensemble sharing is not yet implemented. The maximum message sizes are not shared anywhere. sendMSS is cached and shared in the Apple systems and in Linux. The PMTU is cached and shared in the Apple systems, in FreeBSD and in Windows. The round-trip time is cached and shared in the Apple systems, FreeBSD, Linux and Windows, and its variation in the Apple systems, FreeBSD and Windows. The TCP Fast Open information is cached and shared in the Apple systems, Linux and Windows, and a record of a Fast Open failure is cached in the Apple systems. The send-side congestion window is not shared, and the slow-start threshold is cached and shared in the Apple systems, in FreeBSD and in Linux, with a note that in FreeBSD the new value is the mean of the current and previous values, and in Linux the calculation depends on state and is the maximum of half the current window and the old threshold in most cases.

The document also records what changed since RFC 2140: it clarifies the previous description and terminology, extends the mechanism to its impact on new protocols and mechanisms including Multipath TCP, Fast Open, packetization-layer path MTU discovery, NAT and the TCP Authentication Option, and adds sections on compatibility issues and implementation observations. It also adds an appendix on using temporal sharing over long timescales to adapt TCP's initial window automatically, and expands the referenced literature.
sections.plainLanguage: Several operating systems already do part of this: they remember the round-trip time and the path MTU for a host and reuse them. Few share the congestion window, and the harder case of sharing between concurrent connections is not implemented at all.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The implementation methods presented do not have additional ramifications for direct attacks on individual connections, whether connection-aborting or information-injecting. Individual connections, whether using sharing or not, may still be susceptible to denial of service attacks that reduce performance or completely deny connections and transfers if they are not otherwise secured.

TCB sharing may create additional denial of service attacks that affect the performance of other connections by polluting the cached information. This can occur across any set of connections in which the TCB is shared, between connections in a single host, or between hosts if sharing is implemented within a subnet. Some shared parameters are used only to create new TCBs, while others are shared among the TCBs of ongoing connections, and new connections can join the ongoing set.
sections.plainLanguage: Sharing does not open a new way to attack a single connection. It does add one new risk: if someone can feed bad numbers into the cache, other connections on that machine start from those numbers too.

viz.caption: TWO WAYS OF SHARING TCP STATE

cells: The TCB of an earlier, now closed, connection to the same host
The TCB of a currently active connection to the same host
As early as possible, sometimes before a connection closes
Merged with the old value when the connection closes
Updated with an update function such as a windowed average
A function of the sum across active connections and the number of connections

viz.caption: THE KINDS OF STATE IN A TCP CONTROL BLOCK

items.title: Local process state
items.text: Pointers to the send and receive buffers, the retransmission queue and current segment, and the IP control block.

items.title: Macro-state
items.text: Connection state, timers, flags, the local and remote host numbers and ports, and TCP option state.

items.title: Micro-state
items.text: The send and receive window state, the congestion window and its threshold, the maximum window seen, the segment sizes and the path MTU.

items.title: Host-pair dependent state
items.text: Values defined by the endpoint or the endpoint pair, such as sendMSS, the maximum message sizes and the round-trip time.

items.title: Aggregate state
items.text: Values that depend on the total capacity between the two endpoints, such as the congestion window and the current window sizes.

items.title: Option state
items.text: State tied to a TCP option. Some of it can be shared and some cannot, depending on how the option is negotiated.
